summary:
AeroAtlas is an interactive web platform that turns NASA Mars datasets into an immersive exploration and mission-planning experience. Users travel from a 3D Mars globe to Jezero Crater, explore detailed terrain, and plan simulated extravehicular activities (EVAs)—astronaut excursions outside a spacecraft or habitat.

The platform combines terrain imagery, elevation, slope analysis, and route planning with simulated oxygen consumption, daylight constraints, and rover walkback requirements. A mission-readiness gauge helps users understand safety warnings and compare exploration choices. Helmet view enables ground-level exploration, while the EVA Mission Journal records simulated movement, field notes, and telemetry for route replay and downloadable reports. A weather panel presents archived Perseverance MEDA observations with timestamps and source citations.

AeroAtlas makes complex planetary data accessible through hands-on decisions: where to explore, how to navigate difficult terrain, and when to return. It clearly separates measured observations from simulation assumptions, helping students, educators, and space enthusiasts understand both the scientific opportunities and practical constraints of exploring Mars.
details:
AeroAtlas — Interactive Martian Exploration & EVA Survival Planning System — is a browser-based educational platform developed by Team 4 Loops. It connects planetary exploration, scientific terrain analysis, mission planning, and simulated surface operations in one experience.

The project addresses a practical question: how can an explorer reach a scientifically interesting destination and still return safely? A straight line on a map does not explain climbing effort, oxygen consumption, time spent at science stops, or the reserve needed to return. AeroAtlas makes these relationships visible through interactive maps, route calculations, and simulated exploration.

Users begin with a 3D Mars globe, descend into Jezero Crater, and enter an approximately 6 × 6 km Marswalk zone. They can inspect imagery, elevation, slope hazards, thermal context, contours, and the bundled Perseverance traverse. The planner supports science goals, custom stops, walking, and rover travel with walkback constraints. Terrain-aware A* pathfinding works with the EVA model to estimate route distance, duration, metabolic effort, oxygen requirements, and return feasibility.

A semicircular readiness gauge displays READY, CAUTION, or NO-GO, accompanied by explanations and an elevation profile. Users can revise their assumptions and immediately see how the plan changes. EV1 playback and first-person helmet exploration connect the proposed mission to simulated surface activity.

The EVA Journal records actual simulated movement separately from the planned route. Users can pause and resume recording, add categorized field notes, review saved missions, replay recorded routes, and export PNG reports containing terrain imagery, routes, notes, and available telemetry. Mission history is stored locally in the browser using IndexedDB.

The Weather Intelligence panel presents archived Perseverance MEDA observations for sols 70 and 71, including temperature, atmospheric pressure, relative humidity over ice, and wind where available. Sensor selection, observation timestamps, five-minute trend summaries, quality exclusions, and provenance help users interpret the measurements. A separate NASA DONKI panel provides solar-advisory information. Mineral Science explains cited orbital and rover evidence without presenting unverified mineral locations as confirmed discoveries.

The technology stack combines:

• JavaScript ES modules for application coordination and simulation logic.
• Three.js, WebGL, and GLSL for the Mars globe, terrain, cameras, routes, and graphical overlays.
• HTML and CSS for responsive controls, HUD panels, and dialogs.
• SVG for charts and elevation profiles, and Canvas2D for mission-report composition and PNG export.
• Vite and Node.js for development, production builds, and data tooling.
• Python with rasterio, NumPy, Pillow, and SciPy for preparing geospatial assets.
• IndexedDB for persistent browser-local mission records.
• Fetch, AbortController, and browser storage for retrieval, cancellation, and caching.
• Node’s test runner and Playwright for automated unit and browser regression tests.
• Render for frontend hosting, with optional Netlify Functions for the DONKI proxy.
• Capacitor 8 for integrating the compiled web application into an Android project.

The architecture is modular and primarily client-side. The main application controller manages initialization, feature configuration, and transitions between orbit, crater, and Marswalk views. Core modules handle assets, graphics quality, and presentation. Orbit modules render the planet and orbital overlays, while terrain modules manage meshes, mission stops, pathfinding, EVA budgeting, and helmet exploration. UI modules provide controls, readiness information, profiles, and science panels. Shared libraries handle geography, Mars time, MEDA validation, and DONKI requests. Journal modules manage recording state, persistence, replay, and report generation.

Prepared scientific assets are served as static files. Terrain exploration, archived MEDA access, and local mission history do not require a user-account backend or cloud database. An optional serverless function supports DONKI requests; it is separate from the core simulation.

The data flow has three distinct paths:

  1. Scientific-data preparation: Mission imagery and elevation products pass through the Python terrain pipeline, which crops and resamples them into browser-ready textures and heightmaps. A Node.js MEDA builder prepares a pinned archive subset with provenance and checksums. These outputs are stored as images, metadata, and JSON in the public data directory, then loaded by the application.
  2. Planning and simulation: Loaded terrain, user-selected stops, and editable mission assumptions feed the route planner and EVA model. Their outputs drive the displayed route, resource budget, readiness verdict, elevation profile, and simulated astronaut activity.
  3. Recording and review: Movement and available telemetry from helmet exploration or EV1 playback feed the Journal recorder. Notes and samples are saved to IndexedDB, retrieved for history and replay, and composed into downloadable reports using Canvas2D.

The user workflow is: explore Mars → inspect Jezero terrain → choose mission goals and assumptions → calculate and revise the route → run the simulation → record movement and notes → review and export the mission.

AeroAtlas keeps scientific observations, modeled plans, and recorded simulation activity distinct. Archived MEDA observations do not represent live weather and do not change the EVA calculation. DONKI advisories are also excluded from the readiness verdict. Missing observations remain unavailable, and a planned route is never automatically treated as completed movement.

The project’s creative contribution is bringing these capabilities into a connected learning experience. Users can move from planetary context to ground-level exploration while seeing how terrain, time, and limited resources affect decisions. Its intended impact is to make planetary datasets more accessible to students, educators, space enthusiasts, and developers without requiring specialized desktop GIS software.

Scientific traceability, readable interfaces, browser performance, responsive layouts, and clear uncertainty communication guide the design. AeroAtlas is an independent educational prototype, not a certified operational tool. Its readiness categories describe modeled constraints rather than survival probabilities, and its mission records represent simulated activity rather than real astronaut telemetry.
